SUMMARY:Cloud‑Native Edge Connects Space and Earth - Kenichi Omichi & Tsog Nabar\, Mitsubishi Electric
DESCRIPTION:Our company operates across diverse sectors\, including Factory Automation (FA)\, Space\, Automotive\, and so on.\n These businesses serve as the originating sources of critical data\, which we must transform into customer value through DX.\n Because the generated data continuously changes\, data collection methods and their consuming applications must be changed flexibly and on-demand\, which is driving increased adoption of Kubernetes at the edges.\n We need a common edge platform usable across multiple businesses. For instance\, we are currently evaluating how an edge platform initially designed for FA can be adapted for the unique demands of the space industry.\n While the future of space is bright and full of potential\, its harsh environment often means that existing space components are legacy-based and non-cloud-native.\n In this session\, we will discuss how our edge platform can bridge this gap\, transforming non-cloud-native devices (including space devices) into robust cloud-native edges.

SUMMARY:Upstream Kernel Hardening: Recent Progress and Challenges - Gustavo A. R. Silva\, Linux Kernel Self-Protection Project
DESCRIPTION:With the release of Linux 7.0\, Rust is no longer considered experimental. New and safer components are expected to be written in Rust in the near future. However\, the Linux kernel still contains more than 35 million lines of code written in C. This code will remain critical for years to come and\, for the benefit of everyone\, must continue to be maintained\, improved\, and hardened where possible. In the Linux Kernel Self-Protection Project\, we care deeply about this\, and we've been advancing kernel hardening upstream for several years. In this presentation\, we'll review recent hardening efforts and discuss the challenges we continue to face as we work toward our ultimate goal of eliminating classes of bugs and methods of exploitation in the upstream Linux kernel.

SUMMARY:Browser-Based Local LLMs: A Deep Dive Into Llama.cpp’s WebGPU Backend - Masashi Yoshimura\, NTT\, Inc
DESCRIPTION:Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are improving. Recent models such as Qwen3.8-27B\, Muse Glimmer\, and Gemma 4 deliver strong capabilities while remaining practical on consumer devices through quantization. As these compact models become useful for everyday tasks\, local LLMs are becoming a practical choice for applications requiring privacy\, low latency\, offline use\, and user control.\n \n Presented by the maintainer of llama.cpp's WebGPU backend\, this session explores running llama.cpp in the browser. As browser vendors bring built-in AI to the web platform\, browsers are becoming an environment for on-device AI. Unlike browser-managed AI\, llama.cpp provides an open\, mature runtime for running a wide range of open-weight models through WebGPU\, enabling private\, fully local AI in web applications with the freedom to choose models.\n \n It covers the motivation and architecture of the WebGPU backend\, quantization techniques\, WebGPU kernels (including matrix multiplication and FlashAttention)\, performance comparisons with other GPU backends (CUDA\, Metal\, and Vulkan)\, and the challenges of bringing high-performance LLM inference to web browsers.

SUMMARY:Preparing a Mature Open Source Project for Functional Safety: Lessons From Xen - Cody Zuschlag\, Xen Project - The Linux Foundation
DESCRIPTION:Projects like ELISA and Zephyr have helped move functional safety to the forefront of the open source ecosystem. As a mature project with more than two decades of history\, Xen faces a different challenge: how do you evolve an existing codebase\, development process\, and contributor community to support safety-critical use cases?\n \n Using Xen as a practical case study\, this session shares lessons from the project's ongoing safety journey\, from improving development processes and documentation to producing reusable safety artifacts and collaborating across organizations. Along the way\, we'll discuss the engineering tradeoffs\, community decisions\, and practical challenges that come with preparing an established open source project for functional safety.\n \n Whether your project is just beginning its safety journey or is already supporting safety-critical systems\, you'll leave with practical ideas that can help any mature open source community prepare for what's next.

As an open source automotive platform\, Automotive Grade Linux (AGL) is working to turn the SDV vision into a practical and collaborative software foundation.\n \n In this session\, Jerry Zhao\, leader of the AGL Software-Defined Vehicle Expert Group\, will present the latest progress of the SDV-EG and explain how its different open initiatives are coming together within the AGL SDV Reference Platform\, SoDeV. SUMMARY:CIMD + ID-JAG: Easy in PoC\, Hard in Production - Yoshiyuki Tabata\, Hitachi\, Ltd.
DESCRIPTION:As Agentic AI moves from PoC to production\, security and user experience remain central concerns. This transition is making Agentic AI a major testing ground for emerging OAuth and MCP standards. Among the most closely watched are Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) and Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG)\, a key building block of Enterprise-Managed Authorization.\n \n CIMD can avoid registering every agent instance as a separate OAuth client\, while ID-JAG can enable centralized access decisions and reduce consent fatigue. Individually\, both approaches are compelling and can often be evaluated successfully in PoC environments. However\, production deployments require them to coexist within the same architecture\, and this is where previously hidden design constraints begin to emerge. For example\, ID-JAG recommends client authentication\, while CIMD leaves the associated key-management problem out of scope.\n \n How should these pieces be assembled?\n \n In this session\, Yoshiyuki Tabata will show how to read across these drafts\, identify the hidden constraints that emerge between them\, and turn them into a secure\, scalable\, and usable production architecture.

SUMMARY:The Next Promise: Sustaining the Open Source Base Layer Through Collaboration in the AI Era - Yoshitake Kobayashi\, Toshiba Corporation / CIP
DESCRIPTION:In 2026\, the Civil Infrastructure Platform (CIP) fulfilled its founding promise: a full 10-year support lifecycle for the CIP Super Long-Term Support (SLTS) Kernel\, and became the first OSS project to conform to both IEC 62443-4-1 and 4-2. These milestones showed that long-term sustainability and security can be achieved through industry-wide collaboration.\n \n A year ago at this event\, we spoke of moving "towards" this decade. Now we ask what comes after the first promise.\n \n As AI accelerates software development\, systems such as railways\, energy\, and industrial automation still depend on software that must remain secure and maintainable for decades. The Open Source Base Layer (OSBL) beneath them cannot rely on rapid innovation alone\; it requires long-term stewardship and sustained collaboration.\n \n This talk shares the direction currently being discussed within CIP\, including future SLTS Kernel strategies\, the evolution of CIP Core\, and AI's growing role in large-scale maintenance. While AI is becoming indispensable for sustaining long-lived software\, long-term commitments ultimately depend on industry collaboration—the approach that enabled CIP's first decade and will shape its next.

SUMMARY:Beyond Pass/Fail: Kernel Testing for Developers\, Applications\, AI - Arisu Tachibana\, Cybertrust Japan Co.\, Ltd.
DESCRIPTION:Linux kernel testing produces large amounts of data\, but turning those results into useful decisions and making them accessible outside a single CLI or dashboard is a harder problem.\n \n This talk presents the evolution of kci-dev into a reusable interface to KernelCI. Alongside regression analysis and CI gates\, kci-dev now provides a Python API that allows applications such as Patchwork integrations\, mail-based workflows\, websites\, and other developer tools to submit or inspect kernel testing without reimplementing KernelCI interactions.\n \n We will also explore its MCP interface\, which exposes the same testing capabilities to AI agents and automation tools.\n \n By sharing common APIs and regression semantics across CLI tools\, applications\, CI systems\, and agents\, kernel testing can become easier to integrate while providing more consistent decisions about regressions\, unstable tests\, incomplete runs\, patches\, and future kernel releases.

SUMMARY:Unifying RL Post-Training for LLMs: One DeepSpeed + Ray Engine\, Many Frameworks - Sho Tanaka\, Snowflake
DESCRIPTION:Open-source RL post-training is fragmented. SkyRL\, Verl\, TRL and OpenRLHF each reimplement their own GPU backends and system optimizations — so a speedup built for one doesn't help the others\, and every framework re-pays the same engineering cost. The open-source Arctic Platform (Apache-2.0) takes a different path: a unified DeepSpeed + Ray backend — training\, log-prob\, and sampling engines — that plugs into existing frameworks rather than replacing them (SkyRL merged\; Verl in progress). This talk looks at why backend portability matters for the open RL ecosystem\, how Arctic's integration model works across dense and MoE models\, and what "optimizations that travel between tools" means in practice — like prompt-token deduplication that removes 80–95% of redundant tokens\, whichever framework you run. The goal: less duplicated infra work\, more shared progress across the open post-training community.

SUMMARY:From Project Quality To Tool Confidence: Applying Open Frameworks To GCC for Xen - Wendi Urribarri\, Open Source Contributor
DESCRIPTION:Safety-critical projects increasingly rely on open-source development tools\, but popularity\, extensive testing\, and mature communities do not by themselves establish confidence in a particular tool use. This talk presents initial results from an open pilot in the Xen Functional Safety Working Group evaluating a defined use of GCC to build Xen software artifacts.\n \n The pilot combines two complementary layers. LLVM Qualification Group guidance and templates structure the intended use\, potential compiler malfunctions and consequences\, and technical and process measures. The ELISA Lighthouse OSS checklist examines public evidence of GCC's best practices in governance\, review\, testing\, releases\, security\, documentation\, and sustainability.\n \n Rather than duplicating existing GCC assessments\, validation research\, or commercial qualification approaches\, the pilot treats them as inputs. It does not claim to certify or universally qualify GCC. Instead\, it identifies reusable evidence\, gaps\, compensating measures\, and lessons for GCC\, Xen\, LLVM\, ELISA\, and other communities seeking transparent\, scoped tool-confidence assessments.

SUMMARY:AGL in Production: Development of the Mazda CX-5 Cockpit Domain Controller - Akio Nakadachi\, Mazda Motor Corporation
DESCRIPTION:As the automotive industry transitions toward software-defined vehicles (SDVs)\, cockpit systems are becoming strategic platforms for providing flexible\, updatable\, and customer-centric experiences. The all-new Mazda CX-5 features a Cockpit Domain Controller (CDC) that integrates the instrument cluster and in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) functions on a scalable Linux-based software platform.\n \n This session will present Mazda’s transition from conventional ECU-based architectures to a domain-based cockpit platform that aligns with SDV principles. Topics will include the CDC architecture\, adoption of Linux for cockpit functions\, and use of VirtIO-based virtualization technologies to improve portability\, software reuse\, and long-term maintainability.\n Additionally\, the presentation will highlight how open collaboration and standardization can accelerate the development of the next generation of SDV architectures.

SUMMARY:Carbon as a First-Class Signal: Designing a Standard for OpenTelemetry - Diana Todea\, VictoriaMetrics
DESCRIPTION:OpenTelemetry helps us measure latency\, errors\, and availability. But as sustainability moves into engineering\, one question remains unanswered: how do we observe carbon?\n \n This talk explores Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) through the lens of OpenTelemetry semantic conventions. Rather than focusing on sustainability reporting\, we examine the technical challenge of modeling carbon as telemetry: what entities should emissions be attributed to\, which attributes should be standardized\, and whether carbon belongs in metrics\, traces\, resource metadata\, or all three.\n \n We will explore how carbon-related signals can be collected\, enriched\, and visualized alongside traditional observability data. Attendees will gain a deeper understanding of semantic conventions\, telemetry design trade-offs\, and the opportunities for OpenTelemetry to support a new generation of operational signals.\n \n The audience will leave with these take-aways:\n -Understanding SCI as an observability signal\n -Designing semantic conventions for carbon telemetry\n -Trade-offs between metrics\, traces\, and resource attributes\n -Practical implementation patterns using OpenTelemetry\n -Future directions for green observability

SUMMARY:Certified Today\, Compliant Tomorrow: Keeping the CIP Base Layer Aligned With IEC 62443-4 & CRA - Adithya Balakumar\, Toshiba Software India Pvt. Ltd.
DESCRIPTION:The Civil Infrastructure Platform\, a Linux Foundation project\, took its Open-Source Base Layer through independent IEC 62443-4 assessment — 4-1 and 4-2 — achieved compliance in 2026.\n \n This is a field report on what comes after the certificate. Compliance is not a state a project reaches\, it is a state it must keep across a long maintenance horizon. We'll walk through the routine: continuous monitoring of vulnerability databases\, standing security reviews\, risk and threat assessment with threat models revisited whenever a major update introduces new dependencies and regular IEC layer testing against security requirements. \n \n We'll then map 62443-4 artefacts onto CRA obligation: technical requirements\, SBOM\, technical documentation — and show what downstream integrator's inherit for free versus what they still must do themselves.\n \n Attendees leave with a reusable pattern for making an open-source project certifiable by construction and a checklist mapping 62443-4 maintenance artefacts onto CRA Annex I obligations\, including an honest account of where the two frameworks diverge and what integrator's still have to do themselves.

SUMMARY:Compiler-Armed Fuzzing: LibFuzzer From Userspace To the Rust for Linux - Yunseong Kim\, Ericsson Software Technology
DESCRIPTION:libFuzzer\, the coverage-guided fuzzer built into LLVM\, is everywhere in C/C++ testing yet thinly understood. This talk opens the box: how Clang instruments the code\, how the engine decides which inputs to keep\, and how it cracks magic-value checks it was never told about.\n \n That whole flow\, instrument\, execute\, read coverage\, mutate\, is not tied to userspace. libFuzzer runs in-process: one process both executes the target and reads its coverage\, which is why it is normally used on userspace libraries. Split those two jobs and the same engine drives the Linux kernel: keep the engine and harness in-process\, run the kernel across a syscall\, its high-level interface\, and hand KCOV's coverage back so libFuzzer treats kernel code as its own.\n \n The bridge is a thin layer: a fuzzer is an engine plus a coverage seam\, so the same mechanism serves userspace and kernel alike\, in C and Rust\, with local and remote KCOV and KASAN catching crashes. Understand the flow once\, and the kernel is one more target you can point it at.\n \n [1] LLVM SanitizerCoverage / libFuzzer: https://llvm.org/docs/LibFuzzer.html\n [2] KCOV: Documentation/dev-tools/kcov.rst (Linux kernel)

SUMMARY:Making AI More Reliable With Open Standards - Jean-Georges Perrin\, Actian
DESCRIPTION:Long are gone the days when some thought that AI did not need good data: AI systems are only as reliable as the data and context they can access. Poor quality\, unclear ownership\, missing provenance\, and ambiguous semantics constitute a poor context and turn a powerful model or agent into a very confident source of wrong answers.\n \n Two years ago\, this talk explored why data contracts are good for AI. A lot has happened since. Bitol is now a graduated Linux Foundation project\, and its open standards have evolved from describing data to serving as the ground layer for semantics and context.\n \n In this session\, Jean-Georges “jgp” Perrin\, chair of the Bitol TSC\, will show how open standards such as ODCS and ODPS can give AI systems explicit information about data structure\, quality\, ownership\, provenance\, semantics\, and context. You will see how combining MCP and ODCS is becoming the HTTP and HTML of agents.\n \n Takeaways\n \n * Why reliable AI starts with well-described data and how you can provide that.\n * What's new in ODCS v3.2 and ODPS v1.1 and the features building more trustworthy AI systems.

SUMMARY:Testing the IOMMU Before the Full Stack Exists: Deterministic\, Guest-Free DMA Validation in QEMU - Tao Tang\, Phytium Technology Co.\, Ltd.
DESCRIPTION:IOMMU emulation is usually validated through a full stack: firmware\, guest OS\, IOMMU driver\, workload\, and the QEMU vIOMMU. That makes failures slow to reproduce and hard to attribute\, and a booting guest still does not prove that the translation path is correct.\n \n This talk presents iommu-testdev\, a deliberately minimal QEMU PCI test device that provides deterministic DMA without a guest driver. Qtests construct IOMMU state\, issue a DMA request\, and validate the result through an oracle that bypasses the vIOMMU under test. This turns translation\, invalidation\, fault\, and security-space behavior into an executable contract.\n \n I will show how the same contract is used across Arm SMMUv3 and RISC-V IOMMU tests\, how related helpers are extending toward Intel VT-d\, and how it can support emerging security-aware IOMMU work. SUMMARY:Why Most MCP Tools Fail Silently\, and How To Measure It - Om Shree\, Shreesozo
DESCRIPTION:Most MCP servers don't break because of bugs. They break because the tool descriptions are too vague for agents to reliably pick the right tool.\n Two research papers put numbers to this. Each tool gets a 1–5 per dimension with specific feedback on what's missing and why it matters.\n This talk covers how TDQS was built\, what scoring thousands of real servers revealed\, and how server authors can use it to ship tools agents actually invoke correctly. SUMMARY:BoF: Deterministic ERPC Over SPI - Who Stops the Motor When Linux Freezes? - Robertino Benis\, ReFarm\, Inc.
DESCRIPTION:Edge AI systems converge on a single Linux gateway running inference\, sensor fusion\, networking and actuator control. The boundary is not a best-effort MQTT topic - it is eRPC over SPI with DMA\, giving IPC that survives Linux CPU saturation - hardware-clocked\, not software-scheduled. \n The architecture is displayed live on a D-Robotics RDK-X5 (Horizon J5 BPU) paired with an ESP32 FreeRTOS\, demonstrates three scenarios: \n Traffic Slash: TinyML preprocessing on the ESP32 reduces IPC bandwidth by 90%\, making SPI viable for high-rate sensor data\;\n The Kill-Switch: Linux freezes\, a FreeRTOS Sentinel Task detects the missed eRPC heartbeat\, fires a watchdog ISR and de-energizes the motor relay. We measure latency on an osciloscope. \n Cluster Observability: unified view of Linux processes and FreeRTOS task watermarks\, over the same eRPC channel.

SUMMARY:Transparent Container Startup Acceleration Via CRIU Checkpointing With eBPF Uprobes - Shashank Balaji\, Sony Group Corporation
DESCRIPTION:Container startup latency is a significant concern on resource-constrained embedded devices. We address it by using CRIU to checkpoint a container once\, immediately after initialization\, then restoring from that snapshot on subsequent starts\, skipping the initialization phase entirely.\n \n Our solution requires no modification to the container\, making it suitable for systems where applications cannot be easily modified after deployment. Existing approaches require some form of container modification. Instead\, in our approach\, the user defines the end of initialization as a uprobe location in the container's filesystem (binary + offset). An eBPF program fires when execution reaches that point\, notifies a host-side monitor via ring buffer\, and the monitor triggers CRIU\; all transparent to the container.\n \n We will cover the architecture\, constraints (the uprobe trigger requires a compiled target binary)\, early benchmark results (&gt\; 50% reduction in startup time)\, and a live demonstration. We will also share lessons learned and discuss how the trigger interface can be extended beyond uprobes: file and socket readiness probes being natural candidates.

SUMMARY:Instrumenting AI-Native Applications: OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions for GenAI - Jesús Espino\, VictoriaMetrics
DESCRIPTION:You've instrumented plenty of services: a request comes in\, a response goes out\, and some spans tell the whole story. Now point that instinct at an AI application. SUMMARY:Debugging Embedded Android Display Bring-Up With Linux DRM/KMS: An SPI E-Paper Case Study - Liang-Cheng Wang\, Independent

SUMMARY:Optimizing the CPU Hotunplug for ARM64 Architecture - Tarun Sahu\, Google
DESCRIPTION:I would like to present on my work of optimizing the CPU hotunplug for ARM64 architectures.\n While x86_64 systems leverage parallel CPU hotunplug on kexec/shutdown\, ARM64 CPU hotunplug remains fundamentally serialized in the Linux kernel. SUMMARY:From Packets To Predictability: Evaluating NAPI Processing Models on PREEMPT_RT - Meghana Malladi & Md Anwar Danish\, Texas Instruments
DESCRIPTION:Real-time networking on Linux requires not only high packet throughput but also predictable latency and low jitter. PREEMPT_RT changes the execution and scheduling characteristics of interrupts\, softirqs\, and networking work\, making the behavior of different NAPI processing models particularly relevant for latency-sensitive applications. This session evaluates different NAPI approaches on PREEMPT_RT\, focusing on packet-processing latency\, tail latency\, jitter\, CPU utilization\, and behavior under competing CPU and network workloads. The goal is to provide practical guidance for selecting and tuning NAPI processing models for latency-sensitive real-time workloads on PREEMPT_RT.

SUMMARY:From Documentation to Detectors: Making Zephyr API Contracts Machine-Checkable - Yasushi Shoji\, Space Cubics Inc.

SUMMARY:Designing a New Self-organizing Fetcher for Bitbake - Alejandro Enedino Hernandez Samaniego\, Microsoft
DESCRIPTION:Building a customized Linux OS from source is a complex task. SUMMARY:Software-Defined Genlock on Linux: Synchronizing Distributed Displays Without Dedicated Hardware - Arshad Mehmood\, Intel Corporation
DESCRIPTION:Large video walls and other multi-display systems need their displays to refresh at nearly the same time so the combined output appears as one continuous visual surface. SUMMARY:One .md File for Every AI Agent: Gains\, Losses\, and Costs - Hoon Jo\, KubernetesLab
DESCRIPTION:Every coding agent looks for a filename of its own\, so a project ends up with several context files that say almost the same thing and drift apart each month. An agent that does not read AGENTS.md natively reaches it through an import line or a symlink\, and that indirection inflates the context window you pay for.\n \n So I measured it on one such agent\, across all three paths: direct\, import\, and symlink. Then 210 measurements across five models\, payload byte-identical by checksum.\n \n Two of those questions came back empty-handed. The session then extends the same design to an open-source agent on local models\, so the comparison can be reproduced without a commercial subscription.

SUMMARY:Spec-Driven Development at Scale: Extending Spec Kit Beyond One Feature\, One Repo - Hiroki Ito\, NTT
DESCRIPTION:In spec-driven development toolkits\, coding agents implement from specs. The unit of work is one feature in one repo. System-level QA is hard.\n \n We show what we added to Spec Kit: source of truth at two levels\, feature and system\; interface contracts between repos\; system-level versioning\; and test assets outside implementation repos. SUMMARY:Beyond the One-Line Demo: Seven Lessons From Running Local LLMs - Saiyam Pathak\, vCluster & Saloni Narang\, Kubesimplify
DESCRIPTION:Local AI looks easy in a screenshot: download a model\, run one command\, and watch tokens appear. SUMMARY:Don't Lock It In: Knowledge Circulation With Open Source & InnerSource in the AI Era - Tsubasa Masui\, Mitsubishi Electric Corporation & Duc Nhat Luong\, Mitsubishi Electric
DESCRIPTION:In the AI era\, competitiveness no longer comes from simply owning great technology. Knowledge that AI cannot reach — knowledge kept closed — risks becoming "knowledge that does not exist" as far as AI is concerned.\n \n We started by circulating the knowledge scattered across our organization through InnerSource\, making it reusable beyond team boundaries. This internal circulation is already valuable in itself\, but it need not stop there: open source extend that value outward.\n \n Competitiveness is decided not by the power to enclose\, but by the power to open — correctly. Can you design and publish the interfaces and context that let AI itself reach the unique value worth protecting? Protecting that value is only the starting point\; the real game is in how you open it.\n \n We present a framework using two axes — differentiation and volatility — to decide what to co-create\, what to procure\, and what to build ourselves while opening the right connection points. We then share how we think about\, and have begun working toward\, an "opening strategy" for being chosen by AI\, and the role of the OSPO as the engine that keeps knowledge circulating inside and out.

SUMMARY:Beyond the SBOM: Building a System Knowledge Graph for LLMs With SPDX and Neo4j - Koji Annoura\, Annoura Office
DESCRIPTION:LLM answers can change when the model\, prompt\, or retrieved sources change. At Open Source Summit Korea 2026\, I used the package-lock.json from my Astro website to show how a graph makes software dependencies and changes visible.\n \n Building on that prototype\, this session maps SPDX Elements\, Relationships\, identifiers\, provenance\, and security information into Neo4j Community Edition while retaining their original semantics. Successive SPDX snapshots are connected to operational context\, including Linux hosts and deployed services.\n \n Using Cypher (GQL)\, we will trace dependencies from a package to deployed systems\, examine the impact of a vulnerability\, and compare component changes over time. For LLM-based questions\, a model-independent layer records the model\, prompt\, retrieved graph facts\, source snapshot\, and generated answer\, allowing us to explain what produced an answer and what changed.\n \n Attendees will leave with a reusable data model\, an ingestion approach\, and Cypher query patterns for building this evidence trail with open source components.

SUMMARY:From Display Controller To Panel: A Modular Display Pipeline Architecture for Zephyr - Yash Srivastava & Soumya Tripathy\, Texas Instruments
DESCRIPTION:Modern display hardware is increasingly modular\, combining SoC display controllers\, interfaces such as DPI and MIPI DSI\, protocol-conversion bridges\, and a variety of display panels. Zephyr's current display subsystem is largely vendor-specific\, making it difficult to support diverse display pipelines in a scalable way.\n \n This talk presents a modular display architecture for Zephyr inspired by Linux DRM framework. Display controllers\, bridge devices\, and panel drivers are implemented as independent layers connected through Devicetree. Pipelines are assembled dynamically at runtime\, allowing display controllers to remain agnostic of downstream hardware.\n \n The talk will show how a single display controller driver can support both MIPI DSI and DPI-through-HDMI by attaching different downstream components\, and show how the driver is capable for even eDP and MIPI DBI interfaces.\n \n Finally\, the talk covers hot-plug detection and key design trade-offs while developing the driver for Zephyr.\n \n References:\n Display Driver: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/110013\n DSI Driver: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/114866

SUMMARY:Stop Reviewing Code; Review Context! - Cassandra Chin\, Independent
DESCRIPTION:Classrooms faced the agentic review problem first: when AI can generate a complete project\, source code no longer proves understanding. Software teams are inheriting the same failure mode. A clean diff cannot show which instructions shaped the solution\, what alternatives were rejected\, where human judgment entered\, or whether the agent used stale information.\n \n Most approaches review only the output. This session shifts the object of review. Here\, context is not a larger prompt window\, but the observable provenance of the work: intent\, prompts\, model responses\, decisions\, tools\, and file changes behind the final code.\n \n Using lessons from building Showtail\, an open-source\, local-first provenance tool\, we will examine how to make that context reviewable. Showtail records human-agent interactions\, hashes content\, links events in an append-only journal\, anchors the trail in Git\, redacts secrets\, verifies evidence in CI\, and generates a reviewable report.\n \n Attendees will leave with practical patterns for capturing cross-tool provenance\, designing context reports\, anchoring evidence in version control\, and asking: Did the system act from the right context\, and can it show its work?
